Title: Back to work MD - Experiences of internal medicine physicians returning to work after parental leave
Authors: Hasan, S.; Tang, G. H.; VanderMeulen, H.; Van Bakel, T.; Fralick, M.; Sholzberg, M.
Abstract: BackgroundParenthood in medicine is an experience fraught with challenges that begin in the pre-conception phase and persist as physician-parents navigate their dual role.  MethodsThis study aims to understand the experiences of physician-parents (both childbearing and non-childbearing) returning to work after parental leave. Physicians, including residents, affiliated with the University of Torontos Department of Medicine internal medicine division who had a child within the last ten years were invited to participate in a self-administered electronic survey from June2022 to 30June 2023. Data were summarized using descriptive statistics.  ResultsTwenty-nine respondents took part in the survey; 79% were staff physicians while the remaining were trainees at the time of the survey. At the time their first child was born, 48% were staff members and 52% were trainees. The median duration of parental leave was 5 months (range 1-12 months). Among those for whom lactation was applicable, 76% reported that they continued their lactation efforts on returning to work, while 24% chose not to. Thirty five percent (35%, n=6/17) of respondents cited that they were not provided with duty hour modifications when required. Many respondents (46%) felt guilty about burdening their co-workers for requesting accommodations for childcare. When requested to rate their experiences of balancing their personal and professional lives on a scale of 1-10 (1 being "impossible to maintain" and 10 being "extremely easy to maintain"), most respondents (66%) chose a rating of 5 or less.  ConclusionThis study supports previous findings that physician-parents face a myriad of challenges integrating their roles in medicine and parenthood. A change in culture is required to support and normalize parenthood for physicians and foster sustainability and productivity in academic medicine.

Title: KNOWLEDGE OF METABOLIC SYNDROME, LIFESTYLE RISK BEHAVIOURS AND PREVENTIVE PRACTICES AMONG WOMEN ATTENDING KASOA POLYCLINIC, GHANA: A CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY.
Authors: Aitee, G. D.-G.; Owusu, E.; Cann, A. N.; Borkor, E. T.; Siddiq, A. I.; Kwakye, A. P.; Ampong, E. A. K.
Abstract: BackgroundMetabolic syndrome is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors that may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, and African studies report a higher prevalence in women than in men. Prevention may depend, in part, on whether women recognise the condition and its modifiable risk factors. Relatively little appears to be known about this among women using primary-level health facilities in fast-growing peri-urban areas of Ghana.  ObjectiveTo assess knowledge of metabolic syndrome, describe lifestyle risk behaviours, self-reported cardiometabolic conditions and preventive practices, and examine selected lifestyle correlates of self-reported diabetes and hypertension among women attending Kasoa Polyclinic, Ghana.  MethodsA descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted in June and July 2024 among 174 women aged 18-45 years recruited by convenience sampling. A structured, interviewer-assisted questionnaire covered knowledge, lifestyle behaviours, self-reported diagnoses and preventive practices. Data were summarised as frequencies and percentages, and associations were examined with Pearsons chi-square test.  ResultsOnly 37 women (21.3%) described metabolic syndrome as a condition that raises the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, 40 (23.0%) identified central (apple-shaped) fat as the high-risk pattern and 31 (17.8%) knew that dietary recommendations exist. Most reported no weekly physical activity (116; 66.7%), daily sugary drinks (109; 62.6%), daily processed or fast food (100; 57.5%), high stress (103; 59.2%), and less than six hours sleep (94; 54.0%). Self-reported diagnoses were hypertension in 60 (34.5%) and type 2 diabetes in 49 (28.2%). Fifty-nine (33.9%) had never received advice on prevention and 105 (60.3%) did not monitor their weight or waist. Self-reported diabetes was associated with short sleep (36.2% among those sleeping under six hours; p = 0.035) and with stress level (p = 0.028), being most frequent among women reporting low stress. Self-reported hypertension was more common with high stress (42.7%; p = 0.022) and with some physical activity (p = 0.005).  ConclusionWomen attending this polyclinic appeared to have limited understanding of metabolic syndrome and a high burden of modifiable risk behaviours. Routine counselling on diet, activity, sleep, and weight monitoring at the polyclinic may be warranted. The bivariate, self-reported associations should be interpreted cautiously.
